name: Face rating apps / AI scoring

lead: Face rating apps use algorithms to give a photo a numeric attractiveness score or tier, often on scales borrowed from looksmaxxing such as PSL. People use them to see how a haircut, grooming change, photo angle or other improvement shifts their number.

These tools typically assess features such as facial symmetry, blemishes, wrinkles and estimated age, and sometimes resemblance to reference faces. A well-known early example, the 2016 Beauty.AI contest, judged more than 60,000 entrants; 37 of its 44 winners were white, which critics cited as bias and the company attributed partly to limited data. No validation study of the individual apps was found.

paras: Users upload a front-facing photo, read the score, then retake photos after changes and compare. Many pair it with forum ratings and creator analyses, and keep lighting and angle consistent so the comparisons mean something.

Scores are model outputs that differ between apps and are not clinical measures. Reported concerns include bias from training data and the effect of numeric scoring on self-image; commentators link the wider looksmaxxing culture to body dysmorphia.

angle.text: Users submit photos to apps and AI tools for an attractiveness number or tier, then track it across haircuts, grooming changes and angles to see what moves it. Some convert the result to PSL. Scores are model outputs, and how well they track real-world appeal is largely unstudied.

lead: Face rating apps and AI scoring tools estimate a person's attractiveness from a photograph and return a number, tier or feature breakdown. People in looksmaxxing use them to get a quick private baseline, to see which features score lower, and to track whether changes such as grooming, weight loss, haircuts or procedures move the number over time; some report results on community scales such as PSL.[1][2]

The category draws on long-running research on what faces people rate as attractive: averageness, symmetry, sexual dimorphism, skin quality and perceived health, with substantial agreement among raters across groups.[3][4] Software tools turn some of those cues into measurements such as symmetry, blemishes, wrinkles and estimated age.[5]

A reference point from outside the community is Beauty.AI, a 2016 app-based contest by Youth Laboratories in which artificial intelligence judged symmetry, blemishes, wrinkles, estimated age and resemblance to models among more than 60,000 entrants. Of 44 winners, 37 were white, which critics cited as evidence of bias; the company attributed it partly to limited data.[5] Researchers who study algorithmic bias note that models trained on unbalanced image sets perform unevenly across groups, a point raised in facial-analysis audits.[6]

paras: A Grokipedia entry on looksmaxxing says jawline attractiveness is sometimes rated on a 1-10 scale including by AI tools, and that content creators sell analyses and apps for facial ratings, without naming specific apps.[2] Wikipedia describes the PSL scale as a roughly 1-8 rating created on forum communities, and cites an online page titled "Looksmaxxing Scale: Tiers, Ratings & Free AI Test" as an example of a rating tool.[1]

Typical tools ask for a straight-on and sometimes a side photograph, locate facial landmarks, and compare proportions or features against a model trained on rated faces. Outputs vary by tool, and different apps can return different numbers for the same photo.[5]

Wikipedia says the PSL scale was created on forums in the 2010s, runs roughly from 1 to 8 and rates facial attractiveness only, sorting men into categories from sub-3 up to "giga Chad"; the article describes the scale as pseudoscientific and the forums that created it as defunct.[1] The same article says some men seek appearance ratings on anonymous message boards, and that on some incel forums users rated below average are harassed.[1] Male creators popularised looksmaxxing on TikTok in the early 2020s, and Wikipedia cites a 2026 web page titled Looksmaxxing Scale: Tiers, Ratings & Free AI Test as an example of online rating tools, without describing any app.[1]
Grokipedia says content creators sell facial-rating analyses and apps, and that jawline attractiveness is sometimes rated on a 1 to 10 scale including by AI tools.[2]

Practitioners describe three main uses: a baseline before a change, repeat measurements after grooming, fitness, skin care, hair or cosmetic work, and comparison with reference faces or tiers on community scales.[1][2] Because a rating app can be used privately and repeatedly, some users prefer it to posting photos for rating on anonymous message boards, where Wikipedia says users rated below average are sometimes harassed.[1]

Facial-attractiveness research gives the cues such tools tend to measure. Symmetry raises attractiveness ratings in both sexes, with a larger role in female faces, and symmetry is also linked to perceived health, including healthier-looking skin; symmetry and averageness appear to contribute independently.[3] Computer face-averaging studies found averaged faces were rated more attractive, and clearer, smoother skin is cited as a factor.[4] Researchers also caution that correlation does not establish causation and that mirroring techniques used in studies can create artificial features.[3]

Beauty.AI was run by Youth Laboratories, with Insilico Medicine helping test deep learning methods. Roughly 75% of entrants were white Europeans. After the results, criticism from social justice and computer science backgrounds led to the creation of Diversity.AI, a think tank on bias in AI. The AI also reportedly discarded photos of dark-skinned people when lighting was poor. [5]

Reported figures: more than 60,000 people entered, about 75 percent of them white Europeans, with entrants from India about 7 percent and from Africa about 1 percent. Of the 44 winners, 37 were white, six were Asian and one was dark-skinned.[5] Chief science officer Alex Zhavoronkov suggested lack of data may have contributed, chief technology officer Konstantin Kiselev said the company would widen outreach, and Zhavoronkov pledged to fix the issues for the next contest. The follow-up Beauty.AI 2.0 contest raised age, race and gender bias concerns about deep neural networks, which led to Diversity.AI.[5]

The Beauty.AI outcome is the most-cited example of skewed output: roughly 75 percent of entrants were white Europeans, and the AI reportedly discarded photos of dark-skinned people when lighting was poor.[5] Wikipedia's algorithmic bias article summarises a 2018 study by Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru that found error rates up to about 35 percent for darker-skinned women in commercial facial analysis, versus near-perfect accuracy for lighter-skinned men, which it attributes to under-representation in development datasets.[6] Those findings concern facial analysis generally rather than attractiveness apps, but they are the standard explanation offered for why scoring models can behave unevenly across skin tones and lighting.[6]

Rating apps also inherit whatever beauty standard their training images carry. The facial-attractiveness literature reports broad agreement across raters but also shows preferences that vary by country, for example in how strongly feminised female faces are preferred.[4]

Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article says commentators link communities that rate appearance with negative mental health outcomes including body dysmorphia.[1] Body dysmorphic disorder is defined as an overwhelming preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance, and the condition is associated with heavy selfie-taking and filtered images; cognitive behavioural therapy and SSRI antidepressants are the treatments described as effective.[7] Wikipedia's BDD article does not discuss rating apps specifically.[7]

Wikipedia's article on facial symmetry reports that symmetry increases attractiveness ratings in both sexes, with a larger role for female faces, and that symmetry and averageness appear to contribute independently. It cautions that correlation does not establish causation and that mirroring techniques used in studies can create artificial features. [3]

Wikipedia's article on physical attractiveness reports that a cross-country study found preferences for femininity in female faces varied by country, highest in Japan and lowest in Nepal, and that cross-cultural agreement on attractive facial characteristics has been reported by several researchers.[4]
No studies found validating commercial face rating apps. Related research on facial symmetry, averageness and attractiveness exists but does not test these apps.[3][4]

lore.intro: Rating scales and AI scores are core vocabulary in looksmaxxing: users quote PSL numbers, tiers and tool outputs when discussing progress and features.[1][2]

claims.claim: The PSL scale reflects how women perceive men.
An AI rating is an objective measure of facial attractiveness.
Symmetry is the main driver of a high score.
Tracking a number over time helps motivate improvement.

timeline.event: PSL scale created on the PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net forums, all now defunct.[1]
Beauty.AI contest results announced; bias controversy follows and Diversity.AI is created.[5]
Buolamwini and Gebru study reports uneven facial-analysis error rates across skin tone and gender.[6]
Looksmaxxing spreads on TikTok; AI face-rating pages and apps circulate in the community.[1]
Mainstream media coverage of looksmaxxing increases.[1]
Coverage of looksmaxxing influencers surges in major outlets.[1]
